doc.title: Agentic Workflows: How You Operate
doc.note: This document was written in v2 rather than carried from the frozen v1 estate, so its folder copy is the original and there is no separate layer 0 file. The hash still pins this extraction to exact bytes: editing the prose without re-extracting fails the build. The prose itself is a one-way projection of the founder's memo of 28 August 2026, published verbatim at v2/briefs/45__founder-memo__what-a-workflow-is.md, and the document says so about itself in the section 'Where This Document Sits'.
doc.blurb: born in v2, projected from brief 45; the reference for what a workflow is here

nodes.label: workflow
nodes.statement: A workflow is the set of steps you actually take to get something done, written down or not.

anchor.quote: A workflow is the set of steps you actually take to get something done.

nodes.label: how you operate
nodes.statement: The founder's own phrasing of what a workflow is, and the definition this document adopts.

anchor.quote:
what I call a workflow is fundamentally is how you operate. You know, is the the
steps that you have

nodes.label: agentic workflow
nodes.statement: A workflow in which part of the work is done by something that interprets rather than replays.

anchor.section: Agentic Is Not the Same as Automated
anchor.quote:
An agentic workflow is one where part of the work is done by something that
interprets.

nodes.label: automated workflow
nodes.statement: A workflow that does the same thing every time, and is valuable because it does.

anchor.section: Agentic Is Not the Same as Automated
anchor.quote:
An automated workflow does the same thing every time and is valuable exactly because it
does.

nodes.label: tooling
nodes.statement: The scripts, generators and gates that do the work; the first of the four changeable things.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote: **Tooling** is the scripts, generators and gates that do the work.

nodes.label: visualisation
nodes.statement: How the work is shown back to you; an instrument rather than an output.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote: **Visualisation** is how the work is shown back to you.

nodes.label: comprehension
nodes.statement: What the system can be asked to understand rather than merely transform.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote:
**Comprehension** is what the system can be asked to understand rather than merely
transform.

nodes.label: context
nodes.statement: What the worker, human or agent, has in front of them at the moment of deciding.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote:
**Context** is what the worker, human or agent, has in front of them at the moment of
deciding.

nodes.label: the zone
nodes.statement: The state of attention a workflow exists to protect; the stated purpose of changing the four things.

anchor.quote:
The goal the founder names is a state of attention: to
"allow the author to stay in the zone".

nodes.label: villager phase
nodes.statement: The phase in which a person consumes a workflow rather than changing it.

anchor.section: Two Phases, Not Two Kinds of Person
anchor.quote: The villager phase consumes stuff.

nodes.label: explorer phase
nodes.statement: The phase in which a person creates, customises and fine-tunes workflows.

anchor.section: Two Phases, Not Two Kinds of Person
anchor.quote:
The explorer also will create workflows. Will
customise workflows. Will fine-tune the workflows

nodes.label: reach
nodes.statement: How far into a workflow a person can change things; what experience alters, as against the route.

anchor.quote: What experience changes is how far into the workflow you can reach

nodes.label: the manual-step trigger
nodes.statement: The signal that licenses explorer mode: a step done by hand that should not be.

anchor.section: The Explorer Trigger Is a Manual Step
anchor.quote:
the
signal is a specific felt thing, a step done by hand that should not be

nodes.label: the point of diminishing returns
nodes.statement: The bound on a tooling detour, applying in both directions.

anchor.quote: Every detour is bounded by cost on both sides

nodes.label: payback period
nodes.statement: The horizon over which a tooling detour repays itself; hours or days is acceptable, years is a different project.

anchor.quote:
A tooling detour that pays back in two days
is worth taking mid-project.

nodes.label: maturity
nodes.statement: The state in which running a workflow does not tempt you to change it.

anchor.quote: A workflow is mature when running it does not tempt you to change it.

nodes.label: parked
nodes.statement: A stop with a reason attached and parts already reused; a legitimate state, distinct from abandoned.

anchor.quote: Parked is a legitimate state and is not the same as abandoned.

nodes.label: reusable piece
nodes.statement: A step that can be lifted out of the workflow that grew it.

anchor.quote: The test for a reusable piece is whether it can be lifted out.

nodes.label: source materials
nodes.statement: The things a human authored or a machine captured; the inputs everything else is computed from.

anchor.quote: Source materials are the things a human authored or a machine captured.

nodes.label: projection
nodes.statement: Anything computed from source materials: rendered pages, PDFs, indexes, graphs, summaries.

anchor.quote:
Projections are
everything computed from them

nodes.label: transformation
nodes.statement: Used throughout as the operation that turns sources into projections, and never defined in its own right.

anchor.quote:
what is a
transformation and a projection of those source materials

nodes.label: two-way door
nodes.statement: A deterministic projection: one you can walk back from, or at least rebuild exactly.

anchor.quote: A projection is a two-way door when it is deterministic.

nodes.label: one-way door
nodes.statement: A projection produced by interpretation, which cannot be reversed and whose property everything downstream inherits.

anchor.quote: A projection is a one-way door when something interpreted it.

nodes.label: the deterministic layer
nodes.statement: The side of the boundary the sources must stay on, so that the workflow has a floor.

anchor.section: Keep the Sources on the Deterministic Side
anchor.quote:
the source materials and the source data is all in the sort of the
deterministic layer of this

nodes.label: the folder as the unit
nodes.statement: The convention that a subject gets a folder holding everything about it, tested by portability.

anchor.quote:
a subject gets a folder and the folder
holds everything about it

nodes.label: the chain
nodes.statement: Sources plus chained transformations, which becomes the deliverable in place of any single output.

anchor.quote: the chain itself becomes the deliverable

nodes.label: a named process
nodes.statement: A step given a name, so it can be asked for, stamped onto a folder and checked by a gate.

anchor.section: A Named Process Is Repeatable; a Described One Is Not
anchor.quote:
the name becomes something a person can be asked for, a folder can be
stamped with, and a gate can check

nodes.label: text diff
nodes.statement: A comparison of lines; immediately available and fragile under reflow, rename and move.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote: A text diff compares lines.

nodes.label: graph diff
nodes.statement: A comparison of identified things, able to tell a reworded sentence from a replaced one and to report a move as a move.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote: A graph diff compares identified things.

nodes.label: identity
nodes.statement: Used as the property that lets a sentence survive editing and makes a graph diff possible; never defined here.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote:
If a sentence has an identity that survives
editing

nodes.label: the loop
nodes.statement: The round this document was produced by: memo, verbatim brief, reading, work, gates, narrated release, live page.

anchor.quote: The workflow this document was produced by is small enough to state completely.

nodes.label: gate
nodes.statement: Used throughout as the thing that makes small changes safe enough to be frequent, and never defined here.

anchor.quote: The gates buy speed rather than costing it

nodes.label: everyone already has a workflow
nodes.statement: Reserving the word for automated pipelines hides the fact that everyone has one, and hides the question of whether it is the one you would choose.

anchor.quote:
Reserving the word for
automated pipelines hides the fact that everyone already has one

nodes.label: a workflow is judged by which questions it makes cheap
nodes.statement: The interesting property of a workflow is the set of questions it makes cheap, not its speed.

anchor.section: The Workflow Decides What Questions You Can Ask
anchor.quote:
The interesting property of a workflow is not its speed. It is the set of questions it
makes cheap.

nodes.label: the workflow shapes what you notice about your own work
nodes.statement: Choosing a workflow is choosing the questions you get in the habit of asking, which over months decides what you notice.

anchor.section: The Workflow Decides What Questions You Can Ask
anchor.quote:
Choosing a workflow is therefore choosing which questions you will get in the habit of
asking

nodes.label: the three workflows differ in ability, not effort
nodes.statement: All three authors work hard; only the third can ask what changed between two versions and get an answer.

anchor.section: Three Workflows for Writing a Book
anchor.quote: The three differ in ability, not in effort. All three authors work hard.

nodes.label: four things a workflow can now change
nodes.statement: The tooling, the visualisation, the comprehension and the context: the founder's claim about what is newly changeable.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote:
which is the workflows
that allows us to change the tooling and to change the visualisation and to change the
comprehension and to change the context

nodes.label: the cost of a one-off tool has fallen below doing the task by hand once
nodes.statement: Tooling has been changeable for decades; what changed is how cheap a throwaway script became.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote:
writing a throwaway script is now cheaper than doing the task by hand
once

nodes.label: a view is an instrument, not an output
nodes.statement: A new view routinely finds an error nobody was looking for, which is why visualisation is underestimated.

anchor.section: Four Things a Workflow Can Now Change
anchor.quote:
a view is not an output: it is an
instrument, and a new instrument routinely finds an error nobody was looking for

nodes.label: speed alone is a poor measure of a workflow
nodes.statement: A pipeline that halves the clock but demands attention at three new points is worse for an author.

anchor.quote:
A pipeline that halves the wall-clock time but
demands attention at three new points is a worse workflow for an author

nodes.label: agentic and automated differ in kind
nodes.statement: An automated step can be verified by replaying it and an interpreting step cannot.

anchor.section: Agentic Is Not the Same as Automated
anchor.quote:
an automated step can be verified by
replaying it, and an interpreting step cannot

nodes.label: villager and explorer are phases, not kinds of person
nodes.statement: The founder says phase both times; the same person moves between producing and sharpening.

anchor.section: Two Phases, Not Two Kinds of Person
anchor.quote:
The same person is a villager on the days they are producing and an explorer on
the days they are sharpening.

nodes.label: treating the pair as a personality type produces a lesser version for some readers
nodes.statement: The wrong conclusion the taxonomy reading leads to.

anchor.section: Two Phases, Not Two Kinds of Person
anchor.quote:
Treating it as a personality type produces the wrong
conclusion, which is that some readers should be given a lesser version.

nodes.label: the steps are the same for everyone; experience changes reading speed
nodes.statement: The founder's statement that more or less experienced people go through the same steps at different speeds.

anchor.quote:
sometimes the difference between somebody with more or less experience is just
that they consume materials faster, but they still go to the same steps

nodes.label: one account of the work serves both audiences
nodes.statement: Writing a simple version and a real version solves a problem that was not there.

anchor.quote:
Writing two versions, a simple one
and a real one, solves a problem that was not there.

nodes.label: the default is not to change the workflow
nodes.statement: The founder's instinct is to be productive rather than to improve the tooling, and the detour is allowed rather than sought.

anchor.section: The Instinct Is Not to Change the Workflow
anchor.quote:
my
instinct is always not to change the workflow. My instinct is always, I want to be
productive

nodes.label: the defence against tinkering is a specific trigger, not willpower
nodes.statement: An author who enjoys improving tools will do that instead of writing unless the trigger is specific enough to be absent most of the time.

anchor.section: The Instinct Is Not to Change the Workflow
anchor.quote:
The defence is not willpower, it is having a trigger specific enough to be absent most of
the time.

nodes.label: a tooling detour should pay back in hours or days
nodes.statement: The spoken correction lands on hours and days; a two-year payback is a different project.

anchor.quote:
One that pays back in two years is a different project and
should be recognised as one.

nodes.label: the measure of success is doing a process without changing the workflow
nodes.statement: The founder's stated metric for maturity, and his test for something having been productised or commoditised.

anchor.quote:
the ultimate measure of
success is: Can I do a process without making any changes to the workflow?

nodes.label: maturity is not completeness, elegance, documentation or speed
nodes.statement: The test is only that the workflow survived a real piece of work without needing to be touched.

anchor.quote: It is not that the workflow is complete, elegant, documented or fast.

nodes.label: machinery changes are the price, not the achievement
nodes.statement: A stretch of releases that each changed the machinery is the cost; the achievement is the run where it was left alone.

anchor.section: The Consequence for How Progress Is Read
anchor.quote:
A stretch of releases that each
changed the machinery is not the achievement; it is the price.

nodes.label: an honest account should report the stretches where nothing was improved
nodes.statement: The changes are visible and the not-changing is invisible, so the quiet stretches have to be stated deliberately.

anchor.section: The Consequence for How Progress Is Read
anchor.quote:
Any honest account of a workflow should
therefore report the stretches where nothing was improved

nodes.label: an unlabelled stop reads as a failure later
nodes.statement: Why parked has to be recorded explicitly, including for the author's own benefit.

anchor.quote:
an unlabelled stop looks like a failure
to anyone reading later, including the author

nodes.label: a step that only works where it grew has been used, not matured
nodes.statement: The liftability test applied in the negative.

anchor.quote:
A step that only works
inside the workflow that grew it has not been matured, it has only been used.

nodes.label: projections are created from source materials plus transformation
nodes.statement: The founder's rule for how a workflow scales.

anchor.quote:
you always have a workflow where your source... your projections
are created from source materials plus transformation

nodes.label: the creation of prose is a one-way door
nodes.statement: The clearest case of an irreversible projection, in the founder's words.

anchor.quote: if you think about the creation of pros, it's a one way door

nodes.label: everything downstream of an interpreted step inherits its one-way property
nodes.statement: Once a model enters the chain, the reversibility of everything after it is gone.

anchor.quote:
Every
time a model enters the chain, that step becomes one-way, and everything downstream of it
inherits the property.

nodes.label: the sources must stay in the deterministic layer
nodes.statement: The founder's rule for laying a workflow out.

anchor.section: Keep the Sources on the Deterministic Side
anchor.quote:
it's very critical that,
for example, the source materials and the source data is all in the sort of the
deterministic layer of this

nodes.label: a workflow whose graph is generated from prose has no floor
nodes.statement: If prose comes from a graph the graph survives; if the graph comes from prose nothing upstream is recoverable.

anchor.section: Keep the Sources on the Deterministic Side
anchor.quote:
If the graph is generated
from prose, nothing upstream is recoverable, and the workflow has no floor.

nodes.label: this document is itself a one-way projection, declared
nodes.statement: The document places itself on the interpreted side of the boundary and says so.

anchor.quote: This document is on the wrong side of that boundary, and says so rather than hiding it.

nodes.label: the test of a folder is whether it can be copied elsewhere and still make sense
nodes.statement: If it cannot, the workflow is entangled with the place it grew.

anchor.quote:
If the folder can be copied into another repository and still
make sense, the workflow that produced it can be run somewhere else.

nodes.label: the chain turns a product from a file into something reproducible
nodes.statement: The difference between having written a book and being able to rebuild one.

anchor.quote:
That is the difference between having written a
book and being able to rebuild one.

nodes.label: naming a step is the cheapest reliable improvement to a workflow
nodes.statement: A described step is done slightly differently each time; a named one can be asked for, stamped and checked.

anchor.section: A Named Process Is Repeatable; a Described One Is Not
anchor.quote:
This is the smallest and most reliable improvement available to any workflow, and it costs
one decision.

nodes.label: a diff is part of how you operate, not an extra feature
nodes.statement: Without one, review means rereading everything, so reviews stop happening.

anchor.section: A Diff Is a Workflow Step, Not a Feature
anchor.quote:
Without it, a
review means rereading everything, which means reviews stop happening.

nodes.label: comparing markdown is fragile
nodes.statement: Reflow, rename and move all read as large changes when nothing was said differently.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote:
a reflowed paragraph, a renamed heading or a moved section all read as large
changes when nothing was said differently

nodes.label: the real measure of success is diffing graphs rather than markdown
nodes.statement: The founder sets the graph diff as the test of whether this work succeeded.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote:
you should be delting the diffs of the graphs, not of the markdown. That
would be the really test measurement of our success here

nodes.label: a graph diff exposes whether three earlier things were done
nodes.statement: It is only possible if the decomposition is stable, the identities carry across versions, and each version's graph was kept.

anchor.section: Why a Graph Diff Beats a Text Diff
anchor.quote:
a graph diff is only possible if the decomposition is
stable, the identities carry across versions, and the graph for each version was kept

nodes.label: a formatting-only change is a finding in both directions
nodes.statement: It tells a reviewer what to skip, and catches a change meant to be presentational that was not.

anchor.quote:
It tells a reviewer what to skip, and it catches a change that
was supposed to be presentational and was not.

nodes.label: gates buy speed rather than costing it
nodes.statement: They make small changes safe enough to be frequent.

anchor.quote:
because they make small changes safe enough to
be frequent

nodes.label: versioning buys the diff, which is what makes review possible
nodes.statement: And review is what lets work be corrected rather than defended.

anchor.quote: The versioning buys the diff, which is what makes review possible at all

nodes.label: the workflow does not buy quality of thought
nodes.statement: A workflow of this shape will ship a bad idea quickly, with a good release row and a green suite.

anchor.quote:
A workflow of this shape will ship a bad idea
quickly, with a well-narrated release row and a green test suite.

nodes.label: no amount of machinery changes what happens inside the interpreted step
nodes.statement: The one-way door stays where it is.

anchor.quote: no amount of machinery around it changes what happens inside it

nodes.label: the questions a workflow makes cheap decide, over months, what an author notices
nodes.statement: Stated as a consequence rather than shown; no evidence is offered for the timescale.

anchor.section: The Workflow Decides What Questions You Can Ask
anchor.quote: which over months decides what you notice about your own work

nodes.label: an agentic workflow needs a boundary drawn through it
nodes.statement: Asserted here and argued in Part 5; whether every agentic workflow needs one is untested.

anchor.section: Agentic Is Not the Same as Automated
anchor.quote: agentic workflows need a boundary drawn through them

nodes.label: putting the interpreted step as late as possible is the right general rule
nodes.statement: Argued from one direction of the graph-and-prose case; not shown across other workflows.

anchor.section: Keep the Sources on the Deterministic Side
anchor.quote: Put the interpreted step as late as possible.

nodes.label: allow the author to stay in the zone
nodes.statement: The purpose the four changeable things serve, and the standard a new step has to pay for itself against.

anchor.quote:
A workflow earns its keep when it removes the
interruptions that break concentration

nodes.label: state the principles plainly enough to be argued with
nodes.statement: The document's own stated aim, which is why the principles are numbered at the end.

anchor.quote:
states the
principles plainly enough to be argued with

nodes.label: three workflows for writing a book
nodes.statement: The word processor, markdown with a build, and this repository: the same task done three ways.

anchor.section: Three Workflows for Writing a Book
anchor.quote: The same task, done three ways, shows how much of the outcome the workflow decides.

nodes.label: the bridge and the saw
nodes.statement: The founder's analogy for taking a tooling detour, carrying the payback period inside it.

anchor.quote:
I need a better tool to build this. I go, okay, let me go and build the tool.
Let me sharpen the saw

nodes.label: one round of the loop, end to end
nodes.statement: Memo, verbatim brief, reading, branch work against gates, version, narrated row, validated deploy, live page.

anchor.quote:
A memo is spoken. It is transcribed and published verbatim, transcription artefacts
included

nodes.label: this document's own folder
nodes.statement: The document is an instance of the convention it describes: source, decomposition, extraction and views in one portable folder.

anchor.quote:
this document is a one-way projection of it, and its own decomposition into a
graph is a two-way projection of the prose

anchor.section: Agentic Is Not the Same as Automated
anchor.quote: The difference is not degree, it is kind
None of the four is the goal.

anchor.quote: so I allow myself to go into that explorer mode

empty_sections.why: A restatement of the fifteen principles established above; every one of them is anchored at the section that argues it, so anchoring the summary as well would double-count.
